sit: You are the first forward entering the offensive zone with the puck. The defenseman is backing up quickly. What should you scan for first?
opts: Whether a teammate behind you is calling for a drop pass
The space between you and the backing up defenseman to see if you have room to skate
Whether a late teammate is joining the rush for a pass after you cross the blue line
Whether the goalie is set before you reach the top of the circle
explain: The first read is the defender's gap. If the defenseman is backing up and leaving room, a U11 puck carrier can keep skating and attack the space. If the gap closes, then it is time to delay, pass, or chip to support.

sit: When skating back to retrieve a puck in your defensive corner, you should wait until the puck is on your stick before looking around so you do not lose control of it.
tip: Check your shoulder before the puck arrives.
why: A quick look before the touch helps you know where the forechecker is and where your support is. Then your first touch can protect the puck or move it to an open teammate.

sit: A winger is waiting on the boards for a breakout pass. They stare directly at the puck the entire time it slides toward them, catch it, and immediately get checked.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They stayed too flat-footed instead of taking a step toward open ice
They failed to shoulder check into the middle of the ice to see the incoming pressure
They should have chipped the puck past the defender before trying to catch it
They caught the pass on the boards instead of moving closer to the hash marks
explain: The biggest mistake is not checking inside before the puck arrives. At U11, a winger on the boards should take a quick look so they know whether they have time to turn up ice, need to protect the puck, or should make a quick touch pass.

sit: You are the center supporting your defenseman low in the zone. You see your winger is open on the far boards and you have a clear passing lane, but a forechecker is skating hard at you.
opts: Turn back below the goal line and try to beat the forechecker one-on-one
One-touch pass the puck quickly to the open winger on the far boards before the pressure hits
Hold the puck for an extra second to see if your defenseman gets open again
Rim the puck hard around the boards even though your winger is already open
explain: Because you already scanned and found the open winger, the smart play is to move the puck before the forechecker arrives. A quick pass away from pressure is safer than holding it in a low-danger area of your own zone.
tip: Use your scan early so your pass can be quick.

sit: You are playing defense and catch a pass at the offensive blue line. Before you decide to shoot, what is the most important thing to scan the scoring area for?
opts: Whether a forward is calling for the puck near the corner
If there is a clear lane to the net and if you have a teammate screening the goalie
Whether your defense partner is open for a safety pass across the blue line
If the goalie is leaning before you have checked for blockers in the lane
explain: A point shot is useful when it can get through. At U11, the defender should look for a clear lane and friendly traffic first, because shooting into shin pads often turns into a rush the other way.

sit: You are the first player back for a puck retrieval. Put these actions in the correct order to make a smart play.
items: Collect the puck on your stick with your body ready to protect it
Make a crisp pass to your supporting teammate
Take a quick shoulder check to locate the forechecker
Use your skating edges to create separation from the pressure
explain: The first look gives you a plan before you touch the puck. After that, collect it, create a little space from pressure, and move it to support with control.

sit: You are away from the puck in the offensive zone while your teammate is battling in the corner. How should you use your eyes?
opts: Watch only the puck battle so you can react the moment it comes free
Keep your head on a swivel to find an open pocket of space away from defenders
Drift closer to the corner so your teammate has a shorter pass
Look back toward the blue line first in case your defenseman wants the puck
explain: Scanning away from the puck helps you find soft spots in coverage. If your teammate wins the battle, you are already available instead of skating into the same crowded area.

sit: You are regrouping in the neutral zone. You look up and see the opposing defensemen are standing still at their blue line with loose gaps. What is your next move?
opts: Chip the puck softly into the corner even though you have room to skate
Pass the puck backward right away to restart the regroup
Attack the space with speed to force them to pivot or back up
Slow down at the blue line and wait for them to choose a side
explain: Still defenders with loose gaps are vulnerable to speed. If you scan their feet and see they are flat, attack before they can match your pace.
tip: Flat feet are a cue to attack with speed.

sit: You are bringing the puck up the ice on a rush. You see the first layer of defense stepping up on you. Why is it critical to scan the second layer behind them?
opts: To know if you can chip the puck into space and retrieve it behind the first defender
To see if the far winger is open before you decide whether the chip is safe
To decide if you should slow down and wait for a trailer behind you
So you can immediately turn back and reset the breakout the moment you spot a second defender
explain: Scanning beyond the first defender tells you whether there is usable space behind pressure. If the second layer is too close, a chip can become a turnover. If there is space, an area play can let you keep speed.

sit: When playing weak-side wing in the defensive zone, it is best to stay locked onto the puck so you never lose track of the play.
tip: Scan between the puck and your check.
why: If you stare only at the puck, you can lose the weak-side threat in the slot or at the point. A U13 winger should keep switching their eyes between the puck, open opponents, and their coverage job.

sit: A defenseman receives a D-to-D pass in the neutral zone. They look down to catch it cleanly, hold onto it for three seconds while looking for a pass, and get pressured by the forechecker.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They called for the pass while standing still instead of building speed
They failed to scan up the ice before the pass arrived, resulting in slow decision making
They should have reversed the puck back to their partner immediately
They held the puck in the middle lane instead of moving it toward the boards
explain: Pre-scanning lets the defenseman know the next option before the puck arrives. Without that early look, they spend too long processing after the catch and give the forechecker time to close.

sit: Your team is cycling the puck low in the offensive zone. You are the high forward (F3). You scan the slot and see it is open.
opts: Back all the way out toward the red line to protect against a turnover
Slide into the open high slot, show your stick, and stay ready to recover if possession changes
Skate down below the goal line to make it a three-player puck battle
Stay wide near the boards and wait for a rim or rebound
explain: F3 can become a scoring option when quiet ice opens, but they still need defensive awareness. Sliding into the high slot with a target gives the puck carrier an option without abandoning responsibility above the puck.
tip: Find quiet ice without giving up your safety role.

sit: You are a winger slashing across the neutral zone to receive a breakout pass. Order the steps for a successful entry.
items: Catch the puck in stride while maintaining your speed
Scan the offensive blue line to locate the defensemen's gap
Use the gap read to decide whether to carry, chip, or pass
Present a clear target with your stick to your passing defenseman
explain: The winger should read the gap before asking for the puck. Catching in stride matters, and the earlier scan helps the player choose the entry before the defense can close.

sit: You are a defenseman defending a 2-on-1 rush. What should your eyes be doing as the play crosses your blue line?
opts: Lock only on the puck carrier and angle hard toward them
Look mostly at the puck so you are ready to block the shot
Quickly shifting focus back and forth between the puck carrier and the dangerous pass option
Watch the puck carrier's skates so you can time a poke check
explain: On a 2-on-1, the defender must manage both threats. Scanning between the puck carrier and the passing option helps you protect the middle, take away the most dangerous pass, and avoid chasing one player too early.

sit: You pick up a loose puck in the high slot of your defensive zone. You feel pressure right on your back, but you have not scanned up the ice yet.
opts: Chip a backhand pass toward the middle and hope a teammate is there
Protect the puck with your body and skate toward the safer boards to buy time to look up
Turn back into the slot to keep possession in the middle of the ice
Rim the puck hard around the boards before checking where your winger is
explain: In the defensive high slot, a blind play through the middle is dangerous. If you have pressure and no scan, protect the puck first, move toward safer ice, and get your eyes up before choosing the next play.
tip: Protect first, then scan and move the puck.

sit: A good habit for a center on a faceoff win in the offensive zone is to immediately look back at their own defenseman to make sure the puck was caught cleanly.
tip: After the win, scan opponents and get to your job.
why: Once the puck is won back, the center should quickly find their check, tie up pressure when needed, and get to the net-front or slot area for a screen, tip, or loose puck instead of watching the defenseman.

sit: Your teammate just picked up the puck along the boards. Three players from the other team are skating right toward them to try to steal it.
opts: Skate away from the crowd into open ice and show your stick
Skate right beside your teammate on the boards so you are close for a pass
Stand near the puck and wait to see if it pops loose
Turn back toward your own end in case the other team gets the puck
explain: When several players are already near the puck, skating into the same space makes it harder for your teammate. Finding open ice gives them a clear pass option and keeps the play moving.

sit: You just picked up a loose puck. You look up and see two players from the other team straight ahead of you, but there is open ice on the left side.
opts: Keep skating straight ahead and try to squeeze between the two defenders
Stop with the puck and wait until a teammate tells you where to go
Steer your skates toward the open left side and keep your feet moving
Shoot the puck down the ice before the defenders get closer
explain: Open ice is the safest place to carry the puck. If players are blocking the middle, use your edges to turn away from traffic and skate into the space you can see.

sit: You are in the offensive zone trying to score, but a player on the other team steals the puck and starts skating fast toward your goalie.
opts: Chase the puck carrier from behind and reach with your stick
Stay near the other team's net in case your team steals it back
Glide slowly toward your own zone and watch where the puck goes
Stop, turn around, and skate hard back toward your own net to help your goalie
explain: As soon as the other team gets the puck, your job changes to defense. Skate hard back through the middle so you can help protect the scoring area in front of your goalie.

sit: Your teammate is skating down the wing with the puck and is about to shoot on the goalie. You are skating down the middle of the ice.
opts: Skate into the corner in case the shot misses the net
Stop near the front or side of the net with your stick on the ice, ready for a rebound
Skate up beside your teammate and call for the puck right away
Stop high in the zone and watch the shot
explain: Shots often bounce off the goalie. If you arrive near the net with your stick on the ice and give the goalie space, you are ready for a rebound.

sit: A player digs the puck out of the corner right next to their own goalie. They decide to skate the puck directly across the front of their own net to get to the other side.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They skated the puck through the danger area in front of their own net instead of using the boards
They did not skate fast enough while crossing in front of the goalie
They should have stopped behind the net and waited for everyone to leave
They should have passed through the middle to a teammate right away
explain: The front of your own net is a dangerous place to lose the puck. A safer U7 habit is to turn up the boards or use the wall instead of carrying the puck across the scoring area.

sit: You are stickhandling up the ice, but you accidentally lose the puck off the toe of your blade. It is sitting just a few feet away from you.
opts: Keep skating forward in a wide turn so you can come back around for it
Stop, pivot, and get right back on the puck before anyone else can reach it
Slow down and wait for a teammate to pick it up
Look down at your stick before you chase the puck
explain: Everyone loses the puck sometimes. The best response is to stop quickly, turn back, and compete for it right away instead of making a wide turn.

sit: When the puck is sliding slowly into the corner, you should stare right at the puck the entire time until it is safely on your stick.
tip: Take a quick look before you touch the puck.
why: A quick peek over your shoulder helps you see pressure and open ice. Then you can pick up the puck and skate to safety.

sit: Your teammate intercepts a pass and has a clear breakaway. They are skating as fast as they can toward the other team's net.
opts: Coast near center ice and watch the shot
Turn toward the bench because the play is far away
Stop at the blue line so you do not get too close
Skate hard behind them to follow up on the play
explain: A breakaway can still create a rebound or loose puck. Following the play hard puts you close enough to help if the goalie makes the save.

sit: A player on the other team has the puck directly behind your net. You are the only defender back.
opts: Stay in front of your goalie with your stick on the ice to protect the scoring area
Chase the player all the way behind the net to try to steal the puck
Stand beside one post and only watch the puck carrier
Skate toward the corner boards before the puck carrier comes out
explain: A player behind the net is most dangerous when they pass or skate out front. Staying in the scoring area helps you protect your goalie and the middle of the ice.

sit: You are standing in open ice. Your teammate has the puck and looks right at you. You want them to pass it.
opts: Yell loudly while your stick blade is off the ice
Hold your stick near your skates without showing a clear target
Turn away and skate into space where they cannot see your stick
Tap your stick blade flat on the ice where you want the puck
explain: A good pass needs a clear target. Put your blade flat on the ice so your teammate knows where to send the puck and you are ready to catch it.

sit: You shoot the puck, and the goalie catches it in their glove. The referee blows the whistle.
opts: Keep skating in and try to poke the puck loose before the goalie covers it
Stop right away, turn away from the goalie, and get ready for the next play
Skate through the crease to see if the puck falls out
Stand beside the goalie and wait for the referee to drop the puck there
explain: The whistle means the play is stopped. Good players stop right away, respect the goalie, and get ready for the next faceoff.

sit: You skate into the offensive zone and see that two of your teammates are already in the right corner trying to get the puck from a defender.
opts: Skate into the right corner to make it three teammates near the same puck
Skate all the way back into your own defensive zone
Skate to the front of the net or the open left side and get your stick ready
Stand right behind your two teammates in the corner
explain: If two teammates are already near the puck, they need a passing option more than another player in the same space. Find open ice and be ready when they win it.

sit: The other team is attacking, but your goalie makes a save and the puck goes out to your defenseman.
opts: Turn up the ice, start skating forward, and look back for a pass
Stay in front of your goalie in case the puck comes back
Skate slowly sideways and wait for your defenseman to carry it
Skate into the same corner as your defenseman
explain: When your team gets the puck, you can help start offense. Skate up ice with your stick ready so your defenseman has a forward passing option.

sit: An attacker is skating fast right at you with the puck. You are the last defender back.
opts: Reach only for the puck and let your body drift to one side
Keep your body between the attacker and your net, steering them toward the boards
Back straight into your goalie so you do not get beaten
Skate straight at the attacker and guess which way they will go
explain: The last defender should protect the middle first. Keep your body between the puck carrier and your net, then guide them toward the boards where the shot is harder.

sit: When you are guarding a player without the puck in front of your net, you should hold your stick high in the air so you are ready to bat the puck if it pops up.
tip: Keep your stick on the ice in the passing lane.
why: Most dangerous passes near the net travel along the ice. A stick on the ice can block the pass before it reaches the player you are guarding.

sit: You get a great pass in the middle of the ice. The only person between you and the goal is the goalie.
opts: Stop skating right away so you can take a big shot from far away
Pass the puck backward even though you have open ice
Skate wide into the corner to stay away from pressure
Keep your feet moving, skate toward the net, and shoot
explain: When you have open ice in front of you, keep skating. Moving your feet gets you closer to the net and gives you a better chance to score.

sit: Your teammate shoots, and the puck bounces off the goalie's pads into the slot. The goalie is down, and a defender is starting toward the loose puck.
opts: Take an extra stickhandle to settle the puck before shooting
Stop near the net and tap the loose puck quickly before the defender gets there
Peel away toward the boards to look for a pass
Wait for your teammate to skate in for their own rebound
explain: Reading the play means seeing that the puck is loose and time is short. With the goalie down and a defender coming, a quick rebound touch is better than waiting or taking a big wind-up.

sit: When you are defending a 2-on-1 rush, you should always chase straight at the player with the puck and reach for it.
why: If you chase only the puck carrier, they can pass to the open teammate. A U9 defender should protect the middle and try to take away the dangerous pass.

sit: A player is standing by the boards waiting for a pass. The puck is passed, but it hits a skate and bounces into open ice. The player stays on the boards and waits.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They should have stayed on the boards and called louder for the same pass
They stood still instead of reading the bounce and skating to the open ice to get the puck
They should have backed up toward their own zone before going after the puck
They moved their stick blade on the ice too early
explain: Pucks do not always come straight to your stick. Reading the play means reacting when the puck changes direction and skating to the loose puck first.

sit: You are skating up the ice, and a teammate with the puck is skating right beside you. A defender steps up to block your teammate.
opts: Slow down beside your teammate and wait for them to beat the defender
Skate directly behind your teammate and hope for a drop pass in the same traffic
Skate away from the defender into an open lane so your teammate has a clear pass
Cut in front of your teammate and skate toward the puck
explain: When the defender steps up to your teammate, open ice appears beside or behind that pressure. Moving into that lane gives your teammate a simple pass option.

sit: Your defenseman has the puck behind your net, looking to pass it up the ice to you. The other team's winger is standing right between you and your defenseman.
opts: Stay exactly where you are and tap your stick on the ice
Skate to an open pocket of ice where the winger is not blocking the pass
Skate closer to the boards where the winger is already blocking the lane
Turn up ice without looking back for the puck
explain: If a defender is standing in the passing lane, your teammate cannot pass through them. Move your feet to make a clear lane and show your stick as a target.

sit: You are leading a 2-on-1 rush toward the net. The only defender slides over to block your pass, leaving you a clear path to the goalie.
opts: Try to force a pass through the defender's skates to your teammate anyway
Slow down and wait for the defender to choose again
Skate toward the net and take a quick shot yourself
Dump the puck into the corner even though you have a shooting lane
explain: Good decision making means taking what the defender gives you. If the defender takes away the pass, use the open lane and shoot quickly.

sit: If the middle of the ice is clogged with three defenders, the best decision is to put your head down and try to stickhandle straight through them.
why: Skating into a crowd usually gives the puck away. A better U9 decision is to move the puck or skate toward open space away from the traffic.

sit: A player receives a pass near the other team's net. The goalie is out of position, and no defender is between the player and the open net. The player passes the puck back to their defenseman at the blue line.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They passed away from an open net instead of shooting quickly
They should have waited longer to see if a defender would arrive
They should have skated behind the net to keep the puck safe
They should have passed into the corner before looking at the net
explain: In this play, the best chance is already there. When you are close to the net, the goalie is out of position, and the lane is open, shoot before the chance disappears.

sit: You pick up the puck in your defensive corner. You look up the boards and see a defender waiting there to pressure you.
opts: Skate the puck right across the front of your own goalie
Stop, turn back, and skate behind your own net to use the open ice on the other side
Force the puck up the boards straight into the defender
Throw a blind pass through the middle of your zone
explain: If the boards are blocked, do not force the puck into pressure. Turning behind your net, when that side is open, keeps the puck away from the dangerous middle.
tip: Use the open side of the ice.

sit: Your teammate is battling for the puck on the boards. You are open in the slot. The puck pops right to you.
opts: Shoot the puck right away before the defenders can react
Pass the puck back into the pile of players on the boards
Stickhandle toward the boards to make a safer play
Stop and wait for the goalie to get set
explain: When the puck pops to you in the scoring area, make a quick decision. Shooting right away uses the surprise before defenders can close the space.

sit: You are carrying the puck up the ice and see three defenders waiting at their blue line. Your teammate is skating fast into open ice on the outside wing.
opts: Try to stickhandle straight through all three defenders by yourself
Pass the puck to your teammate in the open space before you reach the defenders
Slow down at the blue line until a defender comes closer
Turn around and skate all the way back to your own net
explain: The middle is crowded, but the outside has space. Passing before the pressure reaches you helps your team keep speed and avoid the traffic.

sit: If a defender is chasing you in open ice, gliding with both feet still is the best way to keep your space.
why: Gliding lets the defender catch up. Keep your feet moving, or make a quick turn into open ice, so you protect the space you have.

sit: A player has the puck and open ice in front of them. No defender is close, but they panic and slap the puck down the ice to no one.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They did not wait for a defender before making a play
They gave the puck away instead of carrying it into the open space
They should have passed backward right away even with open ice ahead
They should have taken a big shot from far away
explain: When you have time and open ice, use it. Carrying the puck forward gives your team a better chance than throwing it away with no pressure on you.

sit: You are on defense in your own zone. The puck comes to you, and you have plenty of time and space. No forechecker is near you.
opts: Panic and ice the puck all the way down the rink
Keep your head up, skate forward into space, and make a good pass
Stand still with the puck until a forechecker arrives
Throw a blind pass through the middle of your zone
explain: If you have time and space, use it. Moving your feet with your head up helps you make a controlled play instead of giving the puck away.

sit: Your teammate wins a faceoff in the offensive zone. The puck slides to you at the blue line, and you have a clear lane to the net.
opts: Hold the puck until a defender gets close
Take a quick step into the open lane and shoot before the space closes
Pass to a covered teammate along the boards
Skate all the way into the corner with the puck
explain: Open lanes can close quickly after a faceoff. A quick step and shot uses the space before defenders can block the puck.

sit: You get the puck behind the other team's net. A defender chases you around the right side and cuts off your path.
opts: Keep skating the same way and hope you can outrun the defender along the boards
Stop quickly, protect the puck, and go back out the left side where the ice is open
Throw the puck to the front of the net without looking
Freeze behind the net and wait for the defender to take the puck
explain: When one side is blocked, change direction to the open side. A quick stop, puck protection, and turn can use the net as a shield.

sit: If a defender's stick blocks the direct pass and your teammate is near the boards, banking the puck softly off the boards can be a creative way to pass.
why: The boards can help you move the puck around a defender's stick. At U9, a soft bank pass is a simple creative play when the direct lane is blocked.

sit: A player is stuck in the corner with a defender reaching for the puck. Instead of turning their body to protect it, they face the defender directly and try to stickhandle.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They exposed the puck to the defender instead of using their body as a shield
They should have passed blindly through the middle right away
They should have shot from the corner before protecting the puck
They should have stopped moving their feet completely
explain: Under pressure, your body can protect the puck. Turning sideways or away from the defender keeps the puck safer and gives you time to find help.

sit: You are skating up the wing, and a defender steps up right in front of you. Your teammate is skating into open ice behind the defender.
opts: Try to skate straight through the defender with the puck
Chip the puck softly off the boards into space for your teammate
Stop and wait for the defender to take the puck
Turn all the way back without looking for your teammate
explain: If a defender blocks your path, you can move the puck to open space behind them. A soft chip off the boards gives your teammate a chance to skate onto it.

sit: You have the puck in the slot, ready to shoot, but a defender drops down in front of you to block the lane.
opts: Shoot it hard right into the defender's pads
Fake the shot, pull the puck to the side, and take a quick shot around the blocker
Skate backward out of the slot right away
Pass to a covered teammate behind you
explain: When the shooting lane is blocked, change the angle. A small fake and side move can open a safer lane for a quick shot.

sit: Your goalie saves the puck to the corner. Two players from the other team skate toward it. You are the closest defender to your net.
opts: Skate to the front of your net and keep your stick on the ice
Chase both attackers deep into the corner
Stand behind your own net and wait
Skate up to the blue line for a pass
explain: The puck is in the corner, but the dangerous place is in front of your goalie. At U7, the simple read is to protect the net first.

sit: If a player on the other team has the puck behind your net, you should chase them around the back and leave the front of the net open.
why: They cannot score from behind the net. Stay near the front so you can stop a pass or loose puck by your goalie.

sit: Your teammate is skating down the side and is about to shoot. You are skating down the middle.
opts: Skate into the corner in case the puck misses
Stop near the side of the net with your stick on the ice for a rebound
Skate up to your teammate and crowd the puck
Stop high in the zone and watch
explain: Shots often bounce off the goalie. If you stop near the net with your stick ready, you can be first to the rebound.

sit: The other team steals the puck and skates fast toward your net. A defender stops at the center red line and watches them go by.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They stopped skating instead of coming back to help protect their net
They should have chased from behind with only their stick
They should have waited at the blue line for a pass
They should have stayed near the other team's net
explain: When the other team gets the puck, your job changes to defense. Skate back hard and help your goalie.

sit: You are standing in front of the other team's net. Your teammate has the puck in the corner and looks at you.
opts: Wave your hands while your stick is off the ice
Skate right up to your teammate and bring traffic with you
Keep your stick blade flat on the ice as a target
Turn your back and skate away from the net
explain: A good pass needs a clear target. Keeping your stick on the ice shows where the puck should go and gets you ready to shoot.

sit: You are skating down the ice with the puck. A defender is standing still in front of you. The side of the ice is empty.
opts: Put your head down and skate straight at the defender
Stop moving and wait for them to move away
Steer to the empty side and skate past them
Shoot the puck from far away before you get closer
explain: When someone blocks your path, look for open ice. Steering to the empty side is safer than skating into traffic.

sit: When you hear the referee blow the whistle, you should keep playing just in case the puck goes in.
why: The whistle means the play is stopped. Good players stop right away and get ready for the next play.

sit: You dig the puck out of the corner beside your own goalie. A defender is standing in front of your net.
opts: Skate the puck up the boards, keeping it close to the wall
Skate the puck right across the front of your own net
Leave the puck in the corner and skate away
Pass it backward toward your own goalie
explain: The front of your own net is dangerous. The boards are the safer path when you are leaving your zone.

sit: A player gets a pass in the middle of the ice. Only the goalie is between them and the net. They pass the puck backward right away.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They should have shot from farther away
They passed instead of skating toward the net to shoot
They should have skated into the corner to be safe
They should have waited until a defender caught them
explain: When you have open ice and a chance to score, keep your feet moving toward the net and shoot.

sit: You are on a breakaway with only the goalie in front of you. A player from the other team is skating hard behind you.
opts: Stop skating and let them catch up
Keep skating fast toward the net and shoot
Turn around and skate back toward the player chasing you
Shoot the puck into the corner and chase it
explain: On a breakaway, speed helps you stay ahead. Keep your feet moving and go to the net.

sit: You get the puck near the boards. A player from the other team skates at you. The ice along the wall is open.
opts: Keep your feet moving and skate up the boards into open ice
Stop skating and hide the puck between your skates
Pass across the front of your own net
Stand still and wait for help
explain: Open ice helps you escape. Keep moving into the space instead of stopping where pressure can catch you.

sit: If two of your teammates are already in the corner battling for the puck, you should skate into the same corner and stand beside them.
why: If two teammates are already near the puck, they need someone open. Move to space so they have a pass.

sit: You are skating with the puck, but it slips off your stick. It is only a few feet away.
opts: Keep skating in a big circle to come back for it
Give up and let the other team have it
Look at your stick before chasing the puck
Stop, turn, and get back on the puck
explain: Everyone loses the puck sometimes. Stop and turn right away so you can win it back.

sit: Your teammate has the puck on the boards. Two defenders are poking at them. You skate right up next to your teammate and stand still.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They joined the crowd instead of finding open ice
They should have poked the puck away from their teammate
They should have hidden behind the other team's net
They should have skated back to their own goalie

sit: As a defender backing up on a 1-on-1, you should match the attacker's speed early but stay three stick lengths away all the way into the top of the circles.
tip: Match speed early, then tighten the gap.
why: Matching speed is useful, but staying too far away near dangerous ice gives the attacker room to shoot, cut back, or pass. At U13, the defender should close the gap with feet and stick before the rush reaches the prime scoring area.

sit: The puck turns over in the neutral zone. The gold defenseman immediately backs all the way to the top of their crease, leaving the blue line and neutral-zone ice uncontested.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They retreated too far and gave the attacker free ice to build speed
They pivoted backward even though defenders should always sprint forward
They stayed inside the dots instead of chasing the puck to the boards right away
They kept their stick in the lane instead of swinging it at the puck
explain: The mistake is not backing up by itself. The mistake is giving up too much ice. A good U13 defender surfs backward with control, holds a useful gap near the blue line, and steers the rush before it reaches the slot.

sit: Your winger is driving the puck wide down the right side. You are the center arriving late. The weak-side defender is locked onto the puck carrier and has not checked behind them.
opts: Drive hard to the far post to occupy the defender and create a second threat
Skate directly toward the puck carrier and crowd their lane
Stop at the blue line for a drop pass while the rush moves below you
Circle behind the net before the puck carrier has beaten the defender
explain: The far-post drive gives the puck carrier a dangerous target and forces the weak-side defender to turn. That can open a pass to the net or space for the trailing player behind you.

sit: Your team wins a puck battle in the defensive corner. You are the strong-side winger trying to become the breakout option.
items: Scan up ice to locate forecheck pressure, your center, and open space.
Receive the pass on your forehand with your body ready to protect the puck.
Skate low to the hash marks to create a short, clear passing lane.
Make a quick read to bump the puck to the center, chip it, or protect it.
explain: First, move into a useful support spot. As you arrive, scan so you know the pressure and your next option. Then receive the pass cleanly and make the next play without freezing.

sit: When angling a fast skater toward the boards, the best route is a straight line at their chest, even if that opens the middle behind you.
tip: Angle inside out, not straight at them.
why: A straight line can miss the angle and let a fast player cut back or chip behind you. A curved inside-out route lets you match speed, protect the middle, and steer them toward the boards.

sit: The opposing winger is skating up the boards. The gold defender has a good angle to the wall, but their stick is tucked near their own waist instead of taking away the puck-side lane.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They are not leading with their stick to take away the puck lane and inside pass
They are skating the attacker toward the boards instead of letting them cut middle
They are keeping their body inside the attacker instead of chasing from behind
They are matching speed instead of stopping to make the attacker slow down
explain: A good angle needs an active stick. Leading with the stick helps block the pass or touch to the middle while the body steers the attacker toward lower-danger ice.

sit: You intercept a pass in the neutral zone. Two opponents are closing from the middle, but your winger is already moving up the wide lane with open ice.
opts: Make a quick, firm pass to the winger who has speed and space
Try to split the two middle defenders before they close their sticks
Dump the puck in before checking whether the wide lane is open
Turn back toward your own zone and let the counterattack slow down
explain: The middle is closing, but the wide lane is open. Moving the puck quickly to the player with speed creates a counterattack before the defenders can reset.
tip: Use the open lane before it closes.

sit: The other team misses the net, and the puck rims hard around the boards to you. You are starting a quick transition out of your zone.
items: Move your feet and snap a firm pass to the center's tape.
Shoulder check before the puck arrives to read wall pressure.
Cushion the puck off the boards so you have control.
Locate your center curling low as the first support option.
explain: The read starts before the puck arrives. Check pressure, find your support, control the rimmed puck, then move it quickly while your feet are alive.

sit: When protecting the puck in the corner, standing still and reaching with your arms is usually safer than using your feet and edges to change the defender's angle.
why: A still puck carrier is easy to pin. Cutbacks, tight turns, and active feet help keep your body between the defender and the puck.

sit: A forward carries the puck out of the corner. A defender closes from the forward's right side, but the forward keeps the puck exposed in front of their skates.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They failed to move the puck to the away hip and put their body between pressure and puck
They kept moving their feet instead of stopping to shield with only their arms
They stayed near the wall instead of cutting straight into the defender's stick
They looked up ice before the defender was fully beaten
explain: When pressure comes from one side, move the puck to the away hip and use your legs and hips as the shield. That makes the defender reach through your body to get the puck.

sit: In defensive-zone coverage, if the opposing center cycles high and switches spots with their defenseman, the covering forward should chase that center all the way to the blue line without communicating.
why: Blindly chasing a high cycle can pull coverage apart and open the slot. At U15 speed, players usually need to communicate a switch so the defensive shape stays layered and compact.

sit: The opponent's puck carrier is tied up with a gold defenseman in the corner. The opposing center slides into the slot, but the gold center is puck-watching from the faceoff dot.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: The gold center lost defensive-side positioning on the most dangerous slot threat
The gold center should join the corner battle and leave the slot to the weak-side winger
The gold center should drift to the blue line early to prepare for a breakout
The gold center is too low even though the slot player is below the hash marks
explain: The most dangerous player is often away from the puck in the high-danger area. The center has to shoulder check, locate the slot threat, and stay between that player and the net.

sit: You are attacking 1-on-1 off the rush. The defender has a tight gap and is matching your speed in the middle, but the outside lane is open.
opts: Change pace with a hesitation, then accelerate into the wide lane
Force a toe drag through the defender's stick and skates in the middle
Stop completely and wait for the defender to back away on their own
Shoot from the blue line even though the defender is set in the lane
explain: When the defender owns a tight middle gap, you have to disrupt their timing. A pace change can freeze their feet, then your acceleration attacks the open outside lane.
tip: Change speed to change the gap.

sit: You are a forward receiving an outlet pass and preparing to attack a lone defender on a 1-on-1 rush.
items: Push the puck slightly wide to make the defender turn their hips.
Build speed as you receive and move through the neutral zone.
Cut back hard to the middle once the defender leans outside.
Scan the defender's gap, stick, and feet before choosing your lane.
explain: Speed makes the defender respect the rush. Then read their gap and feet, push wide to make them commit, and cut back only after they lean outside.

sit: When backchecking against a fast rush, you should go straight to the puck carrier even if two teammates are already pressuring that player.
tip: Sort the threats behind the puck.
why: If teammates already have the puck carrier, another player chasing the puck can leave the trailer or weak-side attacker open. At U15, the backchecker must scan and pick up the next most dangerous option.

sit: The gold team turns the puck over deep. The first forward back starts hard, then glides through the neutral zone while watching the puck behind them.

opts: They stopped skating hard before recovering to the defensive house
They checked over their shoulder instead of staring only at their own net
They backchecked through the middle instead of veering off for a line change
They avoided reaching from behind and taking a penalty
explain: A backcheck is not done when you can see the play. The first forward back has to keep skating through the middle until the dangerous ice is protected, then sort out the next threat.

sit: You are a defenseman retrieving a dump-in. The forechecker takes an inside angle and cuts off your partner. Your strong-side winger is open on the wall.
opts: Shoulder check early, wheel the puck to the strong side, and make a firm wall pass
Force the reverse to your partner even though the inside lane is covered
Spin blind and fire the puck through the middle before pressure arrives
Hide behind the net until the forechecker leaves the inside lane
explain: The forechecker has taken away the partner reverse, but that opens the strong side. Reading that early lets you protect the puck and hit the winger before the forecheck resets.
tip: Take the outlet the forechecker gives you.

sit: A defenseman has the puck behind your net to start a breakout. You are the center executing a low-support route.
items: Read the forecheck pressure on your defenseman.
Swing low into the strong-side circle to offer a short passing lane.
Receive the puck in motion with your feet already moving up ice.
Scan up ice to locate your wingers before the puck arrives.
explain: First read where support is needed. Then swing low, scan before the puck arrives, and receive in motion so the breakout can continue with speed.

sit: When you receive a pass in the offensive zone with no immediate pressure, one-touching it away right away is usually better than holding it long enough to draw a defender.
tip: Use space to make defenders move.
why: A quick touch can be right under pressure, but with time and space you can hold the puck, force a defender to commit, and open a better passing or shooting lane.

sit: A forward enters the zone with speed on a 1-on-3. Instead of using the open perimeter ice to delay, they attack straight through all three defenders and lose the puck.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They failed to recognize they were outnumbered and did not delay for support
They stayed wide too long instead of cutting into the three defenders sooner
They looked for a late teammate instead of shooting from outside the blue line
They kept possession instead of dumping the puck the instant they crossed the line
explain: On a 1-on-3, attacking the middle is low percentage. The better U15 read is to use the perimeter, delay, and let support arrive so the rush can become a connected attack.

sit: The other team's player is skating down the ice with the puck. You are skating back to help your goalie. Where should you try to skate?
opts: Between the puck carrier and your own net
Right beside the puck carrier while poking from the side
Behind the puck carrier and hope they slow down
Toward the boards even though the net is in the middle
explain: At U7, the big defensive job is simple: protect the middle. If you get between the puck carrier and your net, you make it harder for them to skate straight to the dangerous area.
tip: Stay between the puck and your net.

sit: You are skating up the boards waiting for a pass from your defenseman. The puck is almost at your stick. What should you do right before it arrives?
opts: Quickly look over your shoulder toward the middle of the ice
Stare only at the puck until it lands on your stick
Turn your back to the puck and call for a different pass
Stop moving your feet so the pass is easier to catch
explain: A quick look before the puck arrives gives you a picture of pressure and support. Then your first touch can be smarter.
tip: Take a picture before the puck arrives.

sit: An opposing player is trying to stickhandle past you in the neutral zone. How should you use your stick?
opts: Keep your blade on the ice and pointed toward the puck
Lift your stick high so you can swing down at the puck
Keep your stick behind your skates while backing away
Reach from the side after the player has already passed you
explain: A stick on the ice makes the puck carrier go around a real obstacle. Swinging or reaching late is easier to beat and can lead to penalties.

sit: A fast winger from the other team gets the puck and starts skating up the wide lane near the boards. You are defending from the middle. What path should you skate?
opts: Take a curved inside-out path, match speed, and steer them toward the boards
Skate in a straight line at them and hope they do not chip the puck by you
Back into the middle of your zone and give them the whole outside lane
Chase from behind after they pass you along the boards
explain: Angling is steering. A curved inside-out path protects the middle first, then uses the boards to limit the puck carrier's space.

sit: Your teammate is carrying the puck out of your zone, but two defenders are closing on them. You are ahead of the play. How can you best help?
opts: Curl back into a short open passing lane
Sprint to the far blue line for a long pass through pressure
Skate directly behind the puck carrier in the same lane
Stand still on the boards and yell for the puck
explain: A teammate under pressure usually needs a short, easy outlet. Coming closer into open ice helps them keep possession instead of forcing a risky long pass.

sit: Your defenseman goes behind your net to get the puck. You are the center. The forechecker is chasing hard on the right side. What is your best route to support the breakout?
opts: Swing low into open ice away from the pressure to give a safe outlet
Skate straight up the middle through traffic before the defenseman looks up
Stretch to the far blue line for a long pass through the forecheck
Skate behind the net into the same pressure as your defenseman
explain: The center should read where pressure is coming from and become a nearby escape. Swinging low away from pressure gives the defenseman a safer short pass.

sit: You are defending a 2-on-1 rush. The puck carrier is on the right side and is looking to pass across. Where should your stick be?
opts: Flat on the ice in the passing lane between the two attackers
Tucked close to your skates so you can turn faster
Reaching at the puck carrier while the backdoor lane stays open
Up in the air so you can swat the pass after it is already made
explain: On a 2-on-1, the defender usually takes away the dangerous pass and lets the goalie handle the shot. A flat active stick makes the pass much harder.

sit: Your defenseman is preparing to shoot from the point. You are at the net front. How do you make the best screen?
opts: Stay just outside the crease and move across the goalie's eyes as the shot releases
Stand still inside the crease so the goalie has no room to move
Drift beside the net where the goalie can see the shot cleanly
Turn away from the shot and look only for a rebound after it arrives
explain: A strong U15 screen is legal, timed, and active. Moving across the goalie's sightline at release makes tracking harder while keeping you available for a tip or rebound.

sit: The opposing team cycles high. Their center skates up the boards and switches spots with their defenseman. How should you and your winger handle it?
opts: Communicate the switch, pass off the check, and keep the defensive shape compact
Chase the center all the way to the blue line no matter who rotates behind
Both stay low near the corner and leave the high player open
Ignore the switch and fly out early for a breakout pass
explain: High cycles are designed to pull defenders apart. Communication and a clean switch protect the slot while keeping pressure near the puck.

sit: You dump the puck into the offensive right corner. You are the first forechecker in, and the opposing defenseman goes back to retrieve it. What is your primary objective?
opts: Arrive with inside-out speed, take away the middle, and finish legal pressure
Slow down to guess the pass while the defenseman gets clean possession
Sprint straight outside and over-skate so the defenseman can cut back middle
Peel away to cover the wall before the first pressure is established
explain: At U18 speed, the first forechecker must pressure with purpose: angle inside out, remove the middle, and finish with legal body or stick pressure if it is there. The next layers read the forced play.

sit: You have the puck near the boards. Another player is skating at you from the middle to steal it. How do you keep the puck safe?
opts: Put your body between the player and the puck
Keep the puck in front of you and push the player with your hands
Skate straight into the player while the puck stays loose
Leave the puck by the boards and look for a referee
explain: Your body is a shield. If your body is between the other player and the puck, it is much harder for them to reach it.

sit: You are skating toward the net with the puck. A defender steps in your way, but your teammate is open beside you. What is the smartest play?
opts: Pass to the open teammate so they can keep attacking the net
Put your head down and skate straight into the defender
Stop with the puck and wait for the defender to move away
Shoot through the defender even though your teammate is open
explain: When a defender covers you, a teammate may be open. A simple pass to open ice can beat the defender faster than trying to force your way through.
tip: If you are covered, find open help.

sit: You are the only defenseman back, and two players from the other team are attacking with the puck. Where is the best place for you to be?
opts: Between the two attackers with your stick taking away the pass
Charging straight at the puck carrier and leaving the other attacker open
Inside your own crease with your stick tucked beside your skates
Behind the attacker without the puck so the puck carrier has the middle
explain: On a 2-on-1, the defender should protect the middle and make the pass difficult. That forces a tougher shot and buys time for backcheckers.

sit: Your team loses the puck, and the other team rushes the other way. You need to backcheck. Where should you skate first?
opts: Hard through the middle toward the front of your own net
Straight to the puck carrier on the side boards
Wide toward your bench while the rush goes through the middle
Stop near the far blue line and wait for the puck to come back
explain: The middle is the most dangerous ice. Backchecking through the middle helps stop passes and shots from the house.

sit: You are attacking on a 3-on-2 rush with the puck in the middle lane. What should your first move be as you enter the zone?
opts: Attack with speed and slightly shift lanes to force the defenders to choose
Glide at the blue line so everyone can catch up before you decide
Force a pass sideways before either defender commits
Dump the puck in immediately even though you have numbers
explain: Speed makes defenders back up and react. A slight lane change forces one defender to commit, which can open a shot or a pass to a teammate.
tip: Use speed to make defenders choose.

sit: You catch a pass in the neutral zone and see that the closest defender is far away. How should you use this open space?
opts: Keep your feet moving and carry the puck into the open ice
Pass immediately to a teammate who is already covered
Stop still and wait for the defender to come to you
Dump the puck away before anyone applies pressure
explain: When the defense gives you space, take it. Carrying the puck forces a defender to step up, and that is when new options can open.
tip: Take the ice they give you.

sit: The puck is in the corner. You are a defenseman covering a forward at the top of your crease. How do you establish proper coverage?
opts: Stay defensive side between them and the net, with your stick under theirs
Stand puck-side of them so they can slip behind you at the crease
Watch only the puck and let the forward's stick stay free
Push them into your goalie instead of controlling position and stick
explain: Net-front defense is position first, stick detail second. Stay between the forward and the net, then get under their stick so tips and rebounds are harder.

sit: You are a defenseman retreating in the neutral zone with the puck. The forechecker takes away the middle, but your defense partner is open behind you. What is the smartest play to keep possession?
opts: Hinge the puck back to your partner to make the forecheck shift
Force a saucer pass through the forechecker's legs as the last player back
Skate straight into the closed middle lane and hope the forechecker misses
Dump the puck away even though you have a clean support option
explain: A regroup is about finding better ice. Hinging back or across makes the forecheck move and can open cleaner lanes to attack again.

sit: You are carrying the puck up the half wall in the offensive zone. You have drawn a defender high, and your support forward is cutting down the wall behind you. How do you execute the high cycle switch?
opts: Bump the puck softly into the space you just left for the support forward
Toe-drag toward the middle even though the defender is set on your body
Rim the puck blindly behind the net before your support arrives
Hold the puck high on the wall until the defender pins you
explain: The high cycle uses the space a defender leaves. By drawing the defender up and bumping the puck back, the support forward can pick it up with speed going downhill.
tip: Leave the puck where the support is arriving.

sit: You are a center looping low in the defensive zone to support a breakout. You have about two seconds before the puck reaches your stick. What should your scans identify?
opts: Pressure on the puck carrier, the nearest defender's gap, and your next two options
Only the puck, so you never lose sight of the pass coming to you
The goalie behind you, because they decide your first breakout touch
The bench, so you can decide whether to change before receiving
explain: At U18 pace, one look is not enough. You need a quick map of pressure, spacing, and your next options so you know whether to skate, one-touch, or protect on arrival.
tip: Map pressure and your next play early.
